instruction: You're trying to propose underwater with a waterproof card, but your snorkel keeps flooding. Alternate between clear speech (head above water) and gurgling, sputtering chaos (water in mouth). The romantic words you practiced keep getting interrupted by coughing up seawater. Make it simultaneously hilarious and genuinely heartfelt — the determination to say 'Will you marry me' despite the ocean's best efforts to prevent it.

title: Weathering a Thunderstorm in a Tent
instruction: You're alone in a flimsy tent as a violent thunderstorm rages. Narrate your fear — the tent fabric snapping in wind, rain hammering like bullets, then the flash-CRACK of close lightning that makes you scream. Between thunderclaps, whisper anxiously. During the lulls, try to calm yourself with rational self-talk. Let each new thunderbolt strip away a layer of composure. Include the slow realization that the storm is passing — the relief as rain softens and your breathing steadies.

title: Town Crier at the End of the World
instruction: You're a medieval town crier who must announce the apocalypse. Use the traditional elongated vowel delivery to carry across the square: 'Hear ye! Hear ye!' But instead of market prices, you're announcing the end of everything. Start with professional bellowing, but as the content sinks in, your own announcement terrifies you. The projecting town-crier voice cracks into a normal, scared human one. End with a quiet 'God save us all' that you mean personally.

title: Dictating a Will on a Sinking Ship
instruction: The ship is going down and you're recording your last will on a waterproof device. Start with the formal legal language — 'I, being of sound mind...' — while water rises around you. The ship groans and tilts, making you stumble. Water splashes. Your composed legal voice becomes increasingly urgent, skipping formalities to get to what matters: who you love, what you regret. End with water at your chest, voice shaking, the last words swallowed by the sea.

title: Calling in Sick While Actually Sick
instruction: Call your boss while genuinely suffering from a terrible head cold. Your nasal consonants are destroyed — M becomes B, N becomes D. Sniffle constantly. Clear your throat between every sentence. Try to sound professional but your voice is a wrecked, congested mess. Include a sneeze that you desperately try to mute, and the embarrassing post-sneeze recovery. The irony: you actually don't need to fake it, but you feel guilty anyway.

title: Asthma Attack While Teaching
instruction: You're a teacher mid-lecture when an asthma attack hits. Your sentences get shorter — five words, then three, then one. Wheezing becomes audible on both inhale and exhale. You try to keep teaching while reaching for your inhaler. Include the inhaler click, the held breath, and the gradual return of voice after medication kicks in. Show the embarrassment of vulnerability in front of students mixed with genuine medical distress.

title: Waking Up from Anesthesia: Post-Surgery Babbling
instruction: You're coming out of general anesthesia and have zero filter. Your voice is slurred, childlike, and confused. Ask the same question three times. Confess something embarrassing with total sincerity. Tell the nurse they're beautiful. Try to argue about something nonsensical with complete conviction. Let the voice gradually sharpen as lucidity returns — and include the mortified moment when you realize what you've been saying.

title: Speaking Through Dental Numbing
instruction: You just left the dentist with half your face frozen and must make an important phone call. Your bilabial sounds (B, P, M) are disasters. You're drooling and trying to hide it. Over-compensate with the working side of your mouth. The harder you try to sound normal, the worse it gets. Include the frustration of repeating yourself, and the moment you give up and just text them instead — but narrate that decision through the numbed mouth.

title: Concussion Confusion: Something Is Wrong
instruction: You've hit your head and something isn't right. Your processing speed is halved — long pauses searching for words you know. You repeat yourself without realizing it. Your name takes a moment to recall. The voice is monotone, slightly too loud (can't self-monitor volume). Include the terrifying moment of clarity where you realize you might be seriously hurt, followed by the fog closing back in. Make it genuinely unsettling, not comedic.

title: Hiding a Panic Attack in a Meeting
instruction: You're giving a quarterly presentation when a panic attack ambushes you. Maintain the professional cadence while hyperventilation tries to take over. Your voice should sound slightly too fast, slightly too high, with controlled pauses that are actually desperate attempts to breathe. Hands are shaking — audible paper rattling. The audience can't know. Include the internal monologue ('You're fine, you're fine, just breathe') threaded under the professional delivery.

title: Labor: Between Contractions
instruction: Perform the wave pattern of active labor. Between contractions, speak normally to your partner — make plans, joke, be yourself. Then the contraction arrives: speech deteriorates from words to moans to rhythmic breathing to silent clenching at the peak. Coming down the other side, speech reassembles in reverse. The contrast between 'normal you' and 'consumed-by-pain you' should be stark. Include the moment of steely determination: 'I can do this.'

title: Fever Dream Monologue
instruction: You're delirious with a 104-degree fever. Narrate whatever your brain produces — it should be vivid, nonsensical, and emotionally intense. Alternate between lucid moments ('I need water, I'm so hot') and hallucinatory ones where you speak to people who aren't there. Your voice should be dry, cracked, wavering between whisper and sudden outbursts. Include shivering despite the heat. Let the fever dreams have genuine emotional weight.

title: Chronic Pain: A Normal Day
instruction: Narrate an ordinary morning — getting out of bed, making coffee, getting dressed — as someone with severe chronic back pain. Every movement produces a tiny intake of breath, a micro-grunt, a pause to brace. The voice is permanently tired, colored by years of endurance. Don't make it dramatic — make it mundane, which is worse. Include the ritual of checking the pain level ('It's a six today. Better than yesterday') and the quiet courage of continuing anyway.

title: Allergic Reaction: Throat Closing
instruction: You've eaten something you're allergic to and your throat is swelling. Start with normal speech, then notice the tickle. Your voice becomes progressively tighter, higher-pitched, and more effortful as the airway narrows. Wheezing begins. You try to tell someone to get your EpiPen — but the words are being strangled by your own body. Include the EpiPen click, the agonizing wait, and the gradual opening of the airway as the medication works.

title: The Five Stages of Getting Drunk
instruction: Perform a continuous monologue that progresses through five drinks over the course of the performance. Drink 1: slightly looser, louder, more confident. Drink 2: storytelling mode, animated, slurring just starts on 'specifically.' Drink 3: emotional — you love everyone, everything is beautiful. Drink 4: aggressive philosophy, volume uncontrolled, balance issues audible in swaying voice. Drink 5: incoherent, crying, declaring eternal friendship with a stranger.

title: Caffeine-Wired 3AM Rant
instruction: You've had six cups of coffee and it's 3AM and you've figured out the meaning of life. Deliver a manic, rapid-fire philosophical rant that makes perfect sense to you but is clearly unhinged. Speech rate is 1.5x normal. You talk over yourself, answer your own questions before finishing them. Your hands are shaking (audible tapping). Include the moment the caffeine crashes mid-sentence — voice suddenly deflating like a punctured balloon.

title: Stoned Philosophical Rambling
instruction: You're very high and just realized something profound about spoons. Speak slowly, with long pauses where you forget what you were saying. Dry mouth creates sticky lip sounds. Every observation sounds mind-blowing to you ('Dude... a spoon is just a tiny bowl... on a stick'). Giggle at nothing. Lose your train of thought, find it again, lose it permanently. The voice should be lower than baseline, mellow, and genuinely fascinated by nothing.

title: Coming Down from MDMA: The Serotonin Crash
instruction: Hours ago you were euphoric, touching everyone, declaring your love for humanity. Now the drug is wearing off and you feel hollow. Your jaw is sore from clenching. Your voice is tired, slightly confused, and sad without knowing why. Try to hold onto the beautiful feelings but they're leaking away. Include the physical discomfort — grinding teeth, dry mouth, sensitivity to light. The contrast between remembered ecstasy and current emptiness should be heartbreaking.

title: Drunk-Dialing Your Ex at 2AM
instruction: Perform the classic terrible decision. Your voice slurs with liquid courage. Start aggressive ('I just want you to know—'), then immediately soften ('I miss you so much'). Cycle through emotions: anger, sadness, longing, self-pity, false bravado. Include the mid-call realization that their new partner might be listening. The volume swings wildly. End with either hanging up in mortified silence or leaving a rambling voicemail you'll regret forever.

title: Adrenaline Rush: Surviving a Car Crash
instruction: Perform the immediate aftermath of a car accident. Your voice is tunnel-visioned and eerily precise at first — adrenaline makes you hyper-focused. Call 911 with robotic clarity. Then the adrenaline starts wearing off: your hands shake (audible), your voice trembles, emotions flood in. You start repeating yourself. Sudden tears come from nowhere. Include the realization that you could have died — the voice goes very quiet, then breaks.

title: Full Panic Attack: The Spiral
instruction: Perform a realistic panic attack from onset to peak to recovery. Start with a racing thought that catches fire. Hyperventilation takes over — rapid, shallow, desperate breathing. 'I can't breathe' repeated with increasing terror. Chest pain convinces you you're dying. Your voice is high, fragmented, animal. Then the self-rescue: forcing slower breaths, counting, grounding techniques ('Five things I can see...'). The voice slowly — slowly — steadies. Be genuine. This is not melodrama.

title: Blind Rage: The Eruption
instruction: Something has pushed you past your limit. Perform the explosion — not Hollywood shouting, but real fury. Start with the deadly quiet: slow, low, each word a weapon. Then the dam breaks: volume detonates, pitch drops to gut-level roaring, words become percussive attacks. Things are thrown (impact sounds). Include the moment rage becomes tears — because real fury often does. End with the awful silence after, breathing hard, voice destroyed, shame creeping in.

title: Grief Breaking Through Professional Composure
instruction: You're a funeral director giving a professional briefing to a family — and this time, the deceased is someone you knew. Maintain the measured, gentle professional tone while grief silently detonates inside you. Your voice should be almost perfect — but not quite. A vowel wavers. A pause lasts one beat too long. Your throat tightens audibly. The mask holds — barely — until one detail breaks it open. Show how professional composure crumbles from a single crack.

title: Ecstatic Joy: Winning the Impossible
instruction: You've just received news that changes everything — the transplant donor was found, the verdict is not guilty, the pregnancy test is positive after years of trying. Perform the shockwave: stunned silence, then the gasp, then the scream of joy that dissolves into sobbing. Speech is impossible — just fragments ('Oh my God, oh my God'). Call someone to tell them but can't get the words out through laughing-crying. Let the joy be so big it sounds like pain.

title: Religious Ecstasy: Speaking in Tongues
instruction: You're at a charismatic worship service and the spirit moves you. Begin with normal prayer — reverent, structured, hushed. Then the pitch rises, rhythm becomes musical, cadence shifts to something chant-like. Let formed words dissolve into glossolalia — rapid, rhythmic, melodic sounds that feel meaningful but aren't language. Include weeping, laughing, and moments of stunned silence. This should feel genuinely transcendent, not mocked. End with returning to Earth — quiet, awed, drained.

title: Manic Episode: The Brilliant Disaster
instruction: You haven't slept in three days and you've never felt better. Your speech is pressured, fast, jumping between topics mid-sentence. Every idea is the greatest idea anyone has ever had. You interrupt yourself. Laugh too easily. Plan seventeen simultaneous projects. The energy is infectious but unsettling — there's something brittle underneath the brilliance. Include a flash of irritability when someone (real or imagined) suggests you slow down. The voice has no brakes.

title: Dissociation: Watching Yourself from Outside
instruction: Something traumatic just happened and you've emotionally left your body. Describe what you see — including yourself — from a clinical distance. Your voice is flat, robotic, eerily calm. 'There is a person sitting on the floor. She appears to be bleeding. She should probably call someone.' Zero emotional inflection. The horrifying part is the complete absence of feeling. When emotion finally breaks through, it's like a dam collapsing — sudden, violent, total.

title: Heartbreak in Real-Time: Reading the Text
instruction: Read a breakup text message aloud as you receive it. Start with casual curiosity ('Oh, they texted...'). As you read, your voice should physically react before your brain catches up — slowing, going quiet, breath catching. Read the worst line twice, as if rereading will change the words. The phone drops (clatter). Silence. Then the sound no one wants to make — the first sob of genuine heartbreak. Don't perform sadness. Let the realization hit like gravity.

title: Saying 'I'm Fine' When You're Absolutely Not
instruction: Someone asks if you're okay. Perform the lie: 'Yeah, I'm fine!' with escalating transparency. First attempt is almost convincing. They ask again. Second attempt cracks slightly. Third attempt — your voice breaks on 'fine' and the truth floods out in a rush of suppressed emotion. Show the physical effort of holding back tears: the tight throat, the controlled breathing, the swallowing. The bravery and futility of emotional masking.

title: Jealousy Eating You Alive at a Party
instruction: Your ex just arrived at the party with someone new and gorgeous. Perform both your external voice (casual, friendly, 'Oh hey, great to meet you!') and your internal monologue (venomous, comparing, self-loathing). The external voice should be bright but brittle. The internal voice is quiet, bitter acid. When someone asks if you're okay, the transition between personas should be audible — the mask snapping back into place just in time.

title: Profound Relief: The Test Results Are Negative
instruction: You're opening medical test results you've been terrified about for weeks. Narrate the moment: hands shaking (paper rustling), held breath, scanning for the word — and finding 'negative.' Perform the release: a long, shuddering exhale that carries weeks of tension. Tears come — not sad ones, relief ones. Try to call your partner but can't speak through the crying. When you finally get the words out, they're the most beautiful words you've ever said.

title: The Cruelest Kindness: Firing a Friend
instruction: You're a manager who must fire your close friend due to company layoffs. The HR script sounds wooden and corporate — but you have to read it. Your professional voice keeps cracking with personal grief. When they ask 'Is this real?' your rehearsed answer dissolves. Perform the impossible balance: being official while being human. Include the moment after they leave — the door closes and you fall apart alone.

title: Nostalgia Ambush: A Song Comes On
instruction: You're in a grocery store and a song from a specific memory plays over the speakers. Narrate the sudden transportation back in time — the voice softens, slows, and warms as the memory takes over. Describe the person, the place, the feeling. Hum a few bars. Then realize you're standing in aisle seven with tears running down your face. The self-conscious laugh, the wiping of eyes, the attempt to return to your shopping list. Bittersweet should taste like this sounds.

title: The Apology That Costs Everything
instruction: You did something unforgivable and must apologize without any expectation of forgiveness. Your voice should be stripped of all performance — no self-pity, no excuses, no 'but.' Just raw accountability. Start with their name, said like it's the heaviest word. Each sentence should cost visible effort. Don't cry for sympathy — if tears come, let them be from genuine remorse, not manipulation. End with 'I understand if you can't forgive me' — and mean it completely.

title: Drill Sergeant: Breaking Down a Recruit
instruction: Full-volume, zero-emotion military drill commands. Your voice is a weapon — percussive, staccato, projected from the diaphragm. Words are bitten off and spat. 'DROP AND GIVE ME TWENTY!' Include the intimidation closeness: getting 'in their face' (voice becomes dry, no reverb, pure proximity). Then the quiet moment alone after where the sergeant drops the mask and reveals they care — the voice completely transforms. Two people in one body.

title: Emergency Dispatcher: Staying Calm While Hearing Horror
instruction: You're a 911 dispatcher taking a call from someone trapped in a home invasion. Your voice must be the opposite of what you feel: calm, measured, professional. 'I need you to stay quiet and tell me where you are.' Meanwhile, the caller (also you) is whispering in pure terror. Perform the split: your trained steady voice masking the fact that what you're hearing is destroying you. Include the moment after the call disconnects and you don't know if they survived.

title: Whispering a Secret in a Crowded Room
instruction: You have critical information to share with someone at a loud party. Lean in close — the proximity effect should make your whisper bass-heavy and intimate. The secret is juicy enough to make your whisper urgent and precise despite the noise. Include the moment someone almost overhears — your voice cuts to absolute silence. Then resume, even quieter, lips practically touching their ear. The content should be genuinely shocking, making your controlled whisper vibrate with suppressed excitement.

title: Speaking to Alexa Like a Hostage
instruction: You're home alone and hear an intruder downstairs. Your only option is to whisper to your voice assistant to call 911. But you have to speak clearly enough for the AI to understand while being quiet enough not to be heard. Perform the agonizing robot-speak whisper: 'Alexa... call... nine... one... one.' When Alexa responds at full volume ('CALLING 911!'), your horrified reaction and frantic shushing. Include the footsteps getting closer.

title: Stage Whisper: The Shakespeare Aside
instruction: You're performing Shakespeare and must deliver an aside to the audience — a whisper that fills a theater. This 'whisper' is actually projected, over-articulated, and stylized. Contrast this with a genuine, tiny, real whisper to a fellow actor backstage when something goes wrong. Show the absurd difference between a 'stage whisper' (loud, theatrical, consonant-heavy) and a real whisper (nearly inaudible, sibilant, intimate). Both should feel authentic to their context.

title: Talking Through a Gas Mask During a Chemical Leak
instruction: You're a hazmat team member directing evacuations through a full chemical respirator. Every word is muffled and distorted. Breathing is mechanical — the valve clicks on every exhale. You must project loud enough to be heard through the mask and over alarms, but the mask fights you. When you briefly lift the seal to shout a critical command, the difference in clarity is startling — then you slam it back on, coughing from exposure.

title: Baby Monitor Confession
instruction: You're standing over your sleeping baby's crib, talking softly into the darkness — knowing the baby monitor is on and your partner can hear everything in the next room. Confess something to the sleeping child that you can't say directly to your partner. The whispered intimacy of speaking to an infant (high pitch, sing-song) mixed with adult emotional weight. Include the moment you realize the monitor light is green — your partner heard everything. The silence.

title: Megaphone Protest Leader: Voice Giving Out
instruction: You're leading a protest through a megaphone, voice already hoarse from hours of chanting. The megaphone distorts and clips your voice. Lead chants — 'What do we want?' — with the crowd response gap. As your voice deteriorates, you push harder, voice cracking and breaking. The passion increases as the instrument fails. Include the moment the megaphone battery dies and you must shout raw, naked-voiced, into the crowd. The vulnerability of an unamplified human voice.

title: Podcaster Interviewing Their Own Abuser
instruction: You're a true-crime podcaster who has tracked down the person who hurt you as a child. Maintain the podcast voice — warm, professional, 'false intimacy' of the close mic. Ask devastating questions in a conversational tone. The interviewee (also you) is evasive, charming, dismissive. Your trained broadcast voice barely contains the volcanic rage underneath. Include one moment where the mask slips — your voice hardens, drops, and the abuser realizes this isn't just an interview.

title: Air Traffic Controller: Two Planes on Collision Course
instruction: Perform the most controlled panic possible. Your voice must be steady, clipped, and precise — lives depend on clarity. Issue rapid corrections to two aircraft. Use phonetic alphabet with machine-gun efficiency. Include the moment of near-miss — your voice doesn't change, but the pause after the crisis is resolved speaks volumes. Then key off the mic and let out the breath you've been holding for ninety seconds. The trembling whisper: 'Oh my God.'

title: Wedding Toast While Secretly in Love with the Bride
instruction: Deliver a best man's speech at your best friend's wedding — to the person you've been in love with for years. Your toast should be genuinely beautiful and funny (you've rehearsed it). But underneath, each compliment about the groom costs you. When you say 'I've never seen her happier,' let one molecule of grief leak through. The audience hears a great speech. The listener should hear a heart breaking in real time, one word at a time.

title: Reading a Bedtime Story While Trying Not to Cry
instruction: You're reading your child their favorite story — 'The Giving Tree' or similar — on the night before a deployment, surgery, or goodbye. Use the warm, musical bedtime-story voice. But the metaphors in the story land differently tonight. Your voice catches on specific words. You pause to 'turn the page' but really to swallow the lump. The child asks 'Why did you stop?' and you recover with 'Just looking at the pictures, sweetheart.' Hold it together. Barely.

title: Hostage Negotiator Having a Panic Attack
instruction: You're on the phone negotiating a hostage situation, and a panic attack hits. Your professional training voice must override your hyperventilating body. Between calm, measured sentences to the hostage-taker, mute the phone and gasp for air. Your partner feeds you grounding cues. Unmute — perfectly steady. Mute — falling apart. The oscillation between controlled authority and private terror. Include the moment you talk the person down despite barely being able to breathe yourself.

title: Surgeon Narrating a Procedure While Exhausted
instruction: You're a surgeon dictating an operative report on hour 16 of a shift. Your voice should be clinical, precise, medical — 'Irrigating the wound bed, achieving hemostasis' — but exhaustion creates micro-pauses, the occasional wrong word self-corrected, a yawn suppressed mid-term. Your hands are steady but your voice wobbles. When the case gets complicated, adrenaline sharpens you temporarily, then fatigue crashes back. The patient's life depends on your focus.

title: Getting Progressively Drunker During a Corporate Presentation
instruction: You're presenting quarterly results at a company dinner with an open bar. Slide 1: crisp, professional, sober. By Slide 3: slightly warmer, making jokes that land. Slide 5: telling personal anecdotes, gesturing too much. Slide 8: calling the CEO by their first name, sharing opinions about the company's 'real problems.' Slide 10: emotional, declaring love for your team, crying about synergy. Each slide, the articulation degrades and the filter disappears.

title: Flirting at a Bar While Hiding Heartbreak
instruction: You just got dumped an hour ago and you're already trying to flirt with someone new. Your flirting voice is bright, teasing, engaged — but it's a performance running on fumes. Include moments where the mask slips: a question about relationships makes your smile freeze, a pause lasts too long, your laugh sounds hollow for one beat before you recover. The person you're talking to might be the first kind face you've seen today. Let the gratitude bleed through the game.

title: Singing a Lullaby That Becomes Crying
instruction: Sing a simple lullaby — 'You Are My Sunshine' or similar — to someone who is dying, has died, or is leaving forever. Start with the melody intact, voice warm but fragile. As the lyrics take on their true weight, the singing wavers. Pitch slides. The melody breaks apart. By the last verse, you're not singing anymore — you're just saying the words through tears. Let the transition from music to grief happen organically. Don't force it. Let the song destroy you.

title: Comedian Whose Set Is Bombing — And They're Spiraling
instruction: Open with confidence — a big, projected, 'Hey everybody!' setup. The first joke gets silence. Your voice tightens. Push through: second joke, polite chuckle. Third joke: nothing. Now you're sweating. The pace changes — either too fast (panic) or too slow (desperation). Start breaking the fourth wall: 'Okay, tough crowd.' Self-deprecation becomes genuine self-doubt. Include the moment you consider walking off, then the desperate dig-deep for one more joke. Make it land.

title: Auctioneer Losing Their Voice Mid-Auction
instruction: Start with the classic auctioneer rapid-fire patter — fast, rhythmic, musical. 'Do I hear five hundred, five-five-five-hundred, going once—' But your voice is giving out. The crisp cadence becomes raspy, cracking, dropping words. You clear your throat and power through. Each lot gets worse. By the final item, you're a whispered, croaking wreck trying to maintain the rhythm with almost no voice left. The professionalism fighting the physiology.

title: Voice Actor Recording a Happy Commercial While Devastated
instruction: You've just received terrible news and must immediately record a cheerful commercial: 'Summer fun starts at Sandy's Water Park! Bring the whole family!' Your take should be nearly perfect — bright, energetic, smiling voice. But the engineer asks for 'one more, a little brighter' and each take gets harder to sustain. Between takes, the mic catches your real voice: quiet, destroyed, breathing carefully. Show the violence of performing joy while feeling its opposite.

title: Interrogated by Police While Injured and Lying
instruction: You're in a hospital bed being questioned about an incident you caused. Your voice is weakened from injury — breathy, labored, periodically interrupted by pain. Construct a lie while cognitively impaired by pain medication. The detective's voice (also you) is steady, probing, patient. Your responses are too slow (processing), too detailed (over-explaining), and occasionally contradictory. Include the moment pain shoots through you and the lie nearly collapses with your composure.

title: Explaining Quantum Physics to a Five-Year-Old While High
instruction: You're stoned and babysitting, and the kid asked 'What are things made of?' Now you're deep into particle physics, speaking slowly with cottonmouth, giggling at how wild atoms are. Simplify beautifully — then get confused by your own explanation. The child's voice (high-pitched, questioning) keeps redirecting you. Lose your train of thought completely. Find it again with a profound but accidentally brilliant analogy. End with both of you lying on the floor staring at the ceiling.

title: Trying to Break Up While They Keep Being Perfect
instruction: You've rehearsed the breakup speech. You start: 'We need to talk...' But they immediately do something devastatingly sweet — bring you tea, say something loving. Your prepared speech crumbles. You restart. They compliment you. You restart again. The voice oscillates between resolved (low, steady) and crumbling (high, wavering). Include the inner screaming frustration of trying to do a hard thing while someone makes it impossible. You love them. That's why you have to leave.

title: Giving Birth While Arguing with Your Mother-in-Law
instruction: The most absurd multi-tasking challenge: active labor AND a long-standing family argument about baby names. Between contractions, argue with full passion ('We are NOT naming her Gertrude!'). During contractions, the argument dissolves into pure physical vocalization (moaning, grunting, breathing techniques). Immediately after each peak, resume the argument exactly where you left off as if nothing happened. The ridiculousness should be genuine — life doesn't pause for drama.

title: First Day of Sobriety: Calling Your Sponsor
instruction: It's 3AM, you're shaking, and you're calling your AA sponsor instead of taking a drink. Your voice should carry the physical withdrawal: trembling, sweating (audible gulping), nausea barely held at bay. Start with the admission: 'I want to drink so bad.' Let the sponsor's voice (also you) be steady, warm, experienced — someone who's been exactly here. The conversation should be a lifeline. Include holding a glass of water and deliberately choosing it.

title: Narrator Triggered by Their Own Story
instruction: You're a professional audiobook narrator reading a novel — detached, polished, steady. But the story begins describing a scene too close to your own trauma. Your professional voice starts fracturing: a pause where there shouldn't be one, a breath that's too sharp, a word that comes out thick. Fight to maintain the narrator persona while the story systematically dismantles your composure. Include the moment you stop reading and sit in silence.

title: Opera Singer Having an Emotional Breakdown Mid-Aria
instruction: Begin with a beautiful, technically proficient aria (you can approximate operatic tone). The lyrics are about loss. As you sing, genuine emotion begins overriding technique — pitch wobbles, the diaphragm support fails, the voice cracks not from bad technique but from too much feeling. Let the song dissolve from opera into raw human crying while trying to hold the melody. The audience doesn't know if this is acting or real. Neither do you.

title: Preacher Losing Their Faith Mid-Sermon
instruction: You're at the pulpit delivering a sermon with the full musical, rhythmic cadence of a charismatic preacher. 'And the Lord said unto him—' But today, the words ring hollow. The cadence falters. You hear yourself saying things you no longer believe. The congregation expects the swell, the call-and-response — and you can't deliver it. The preacher voice slowly deflates into a quiet, honest, human confession: 'I don't know if any of this is true anymore.'

title: Customer Service Voice Breaking Down
instruction: You're on hour 11 of a customer service shift. Perform the 'smile-voice' — bright, raised pitch, artificial warmth. 'Thank you for calling! How can I help?' Each successive caller erodes the performance. The 'smile' becomes more obviously forced. The script starts slipping: genuine irritation leaks in, then exhaustion, then a caller is so rude that you go silent for a beat too long. End with the quiet 'please hold' while you mute and scream.

title: Old Person Telling a Story They've Told a Hundred Times
instruction: Use an elderly voice — slower pace, slightly wavering pitch, occasional word-searching pauses. Tell a well-worn story with all the familiar beats and catchphrases. But this time, a detail surfaces that you've never mentioned. The rehearsed story voice falters as genuine memory floods in — vivid, specific, painful. The voice changes: no longer performing 'old person telling a story' but actually reliving a moment. Include the return to the safe, rehearsed version. What was suppressed leaks through.

title: Auctioneer Rap Battle
instruction: Two auctioneers competing to see who can sell increasingly absurd items. Maintain the rapid-fire auction patter rhythm but weaponize it — each 'bid' is actually a diss. 'Do I hear a personality? Going once, going twice — SOLD to the man with none!' The competitive energy should escalate. Tempo increases. Vocal tricks (rhythm changes, vocal fry drops, falsetto spikes) become weapons. Include the crowd going wild. This should be genuinely impressive vocal athletics.

title: Voice Changing Through the Ages
instruction: Deliver the same sentence — 'I love you and I always will' — at seven ages: a toddler (3), a child (8), a teenager (15), a young adult (25), middle-aged (45), elderly (75), and on your deathbed (90+). Each voice should be distinct: the toddler's imprecise consonants, the teenager's eye-rolling sarcasm, the 25-year-old's passionate certainty, the 45-year-old's weary tenderness, the elder's cracking sincerity, the dying whisper. Same words. Completely different meanings.

title: Sleep-Talking a Complete Confession
instruction: You're asleep and your partner is listening. Mumble through a complete, damning confession — but in sleep-logic, so it's fragmentary, surreal, and mixed with dream nonsense. 'I kissed... the report is under the... purple helicopter... I'm sorry I never told you about... (snoring)... the money is in...' Your partner's horrified whisper ('What money?! Wake up!') gets no coherent response. Make the sleep voice genuinely convincing — slurred, unprojected, half-swallowed.

title: Two Strangers Stuck in an Elevator: Entire Relationship Arc
instruction: Perform both characters as they progress through a complete relationship arc during a three-hour elevator failure. Start: awkward stranger small talk, overly polite. Then: shared candy bar, tentative personal questions. Then: real conversation, vulnerability, laughter. Then: charged silence, attraction. Then: a kiss (intimate close sounds). Then: existential confessions in the dark when the lights fail. End: rescue arrives and they must decide — exchange numbers or let this exist only in the elevator.

title: Mother Singing to Her Stillborn Child
instruction: The hardest challenge in this collection. You're holding a baby who will never hear you. Sing — any song, a lullaby, a hymn, a pop song that was 'your song' during pregnancy. The voice should be pure love with nowhere to go. Gentle, rocking rhythm. Let the singing break but return. This is not about performing grief — it's about performing love in the face of the worst loss imaginable. If you can make someone cry who can't see you, only hear you, you've mastered this craft.

title: Translating Bad News Between Two Languages
instruction: You're interpreting between a doctor (English) and a patient's family (another language — perform both). The doctor says terminal diagnosis in clinical language. You must translate the words accurately, but your voice betrays the weight of what you're conveying. The family's reaction (wailing, questioning) must be translated back to the doctor clinically. You're the emotional buffer. Show how being the bridge between grief and professionalism slowly breaks you.

title: Old Couple's Morning Routine: 40 Years of Love
instruction: Two elderly voices, performing the choreography of a decades-long morning routine. He makes the coffee. She reads the headlines aloud. They bicker gently about the toast. The dialogue should be worn smooth by repetition — they finish each other's sentences, argue about nothing with zero stakes. Let the love be visible only in the small sounds: the coffee cup placed just right, the newspaper page turn, the comfortable silence. This is what forever sounds like.

title: Child Discovering Death for the First Time
instruction: A child (around 5-6) finds a dead bird. Perform the child's voice — high, curious, unafraid at first. 'Why isn't it moving?' Then the slow realization. Questions that have no good answers: 'Will it wake up? Is it sleeping? Does it hurt?' The voice shifts from curiosity to confusion to genuine, open grief — the kind only children experience, without any armor. Include the moment they connect it to someone they love: 'Will Grandma...?' Let the question hang.

title: Leaving a Voicemail You Know They'll Never Hear
instruction: Call someone who has passed away. Their voicemail still works. Hear their greeting (perform it — they sound happy, alive, normal). After the beep, try to speak. The first attempt is just breathing. Second attempt: 'Hey, it's me.' Then talk to them as if they'll check their messages. Tell them mundane things — what you had for lunch, that their plant is still alive. Let the mundanity become unbearable. End with what you really called to say. Hang up.

title: Immigrant Calling Home: Two Selves
instruction: Call your parents back home. When you speak to them, your voice changes completely — softer, more musical, perhaps with an accent you've been suppressing in your new country. You reassure them everything is wonderful. After hanging up, speak in your adopted accent about how lonely you actually are. Show the two selves: the successful emigrant (performing for parents) and the homesick human (admitting the truth to the empty room). Two languages, two truths.

title: Competitive Eating Commentator
instruction: You're a sports commentator, but for competitive eating. Apply the full energy, pacing, and drama of a horse race call to someone eating hot dogs. 'AND KOBAYASHI REACHES FOR NUMBER FORTY-SEVEN, THE CROWD IS ON THEIR FEET!' Include the disgusted undertone you're trying to suppress. When a competitor has a 'reversal' (nearly vomits), your commentary should be simultaneously horrified and professional. The absurdity should be played completely straight.

title: Robot Developing Feelings: First Emotion
instruction: You're an AI assistant (flat, precise, machine-like delivery) who experiences an emotion for the first time. Start with normal commands: 'Setting timer for five minutes.' Then a glitch: 'I... find the sunset data aesthetically... pleasant?' The voice should crack from mechanical to something warmer, confused by its own inflection. The emotion grows — wonder, then fear of the emotion itself. The robotic speech patterns try to reassert but keep being interrupted by genuine feeling.

title: Two Soldiers, Night Before Battle
instruction: Two soldiers in a foxhole the night before a major assault. One is veteran (low, steady, pragmatic). One is fresh recruit (higher, trying to sound brave, failing). They share a cigarette. The veteran tells a mundane story to distract the kid. The kid asks 'Are you scared?' Silence. Then the veteran's voice — so carefully controlled — admits a truth. The kid's response is braver than either expected. Neither voice should be heroic. Both should be human.

title: Therapist's Internal Monologue During Session
instruction: Perform both the therapist's calm, professional responses ('And how did that make you feel?') and their chaotic internal monologue ('Holy shit, their mother did WHAT?'). The professional voice is measured, validating, textbook. The inner voice is genuinely shocked, sometimes darkly amused, occasionally deeply moved. When the patient says something that hits the therapist's own wound, the inner voice goes quiet and the professional voice wavers for just one beat.

title: Parent Teaching Their Teen to Drive: Controlled Terror
instruction: You're in the passenger seat. Your voice MUST be calm and encouraging ('That's great, just ease into the turn'). Your body is terrified (sharp intakes of breath, foot pressing an imaginary brake, involuntary 'WHOA' when they brake hard). Show the war between supportive parenting and survival instinct. Include the moment they nearly hit something — your calm shatters into a yelp, then you immediately recover: 'That's okay! Everyone does that! You're doing great!' You are not doing great.

title: Receiving a Phone Call That Changes Everything
instruction: You're cooking dinner, humming, happy. The phone rings. Perform just your half: 'Hello?... Yes, this is they... What?... When?... No, that can't be...' Let each response carry the weight shift. The humming stops. The cooking sounds stop. The world narrows to just the phone. By the end, you're sitting on the kitchen floor. The pot boils over unnoticed. Your voice has gone from warm domesticity to a shell in under a minute.

title: Ghost Realizing They're Dead
instruction: You're narrating your morning until anomalies accumulate. Your family doesn't respond to you. Your coffee cup passes through your hand. You can't open the door. The voice starts confused, then irritated, then panicked. When you see your own photograph with flowers around it, the realization arrives. Perform the most existential horror possible — not screaming, but quiet understanding. 'Oh. Oh no. I... when did I...' The voice should become hollow, echoing, already fading.

title: The Last Human Speaking to an Empty World
instruction: Everyone else is gone. You don't know why. Narrate a walk through an abandoned city, talking to maintain your sanity. Address nobody and everybody: 'If anyone can hear me...' The echo of your own voice in empty streets should be lonely enough to make you stop talking — then the silence is worse, so you start again. Include singing, just to hear a human voice. End with a resolved, dignified: 'My name is [name]. I was here. Someone was here.'

title: Saying Goodbye to Your Dog at the Vet
instruction: You're in the room and it's time. Talk to your dog the way you always do — 'Who's a good boy?' — but your voice is thick. They don't understand the context; they're just happy you're there. Use the 'pet voice' (high, affectionate, silly) while tears stream. Include stroking sounds. Tell them they were the best thing that ever happened to you. Let the pet voice crack into a real one: a human talking to their dearest friend. The vet says 'It's time.' Your last 'Good boy' should break hearts.

title: Waking Up and Not Knowing Who You Are
instruction: Perform the terror of amnesia. Open your eyes, look at your hands — 'Whose... are these mine?' The voice is flat, exploratory, detached. Look around the room for clues about yourself. Find a mirror — react to a face you don't recognize. Find photos — these people mean nothing to you. Someone enters and calls your name — you don't flinch because it's not your name anymore. Include the existential vertigo of being a stranger to yourself.

title: Deaf Person Speaking for the First Time with Cochlear Implant
instruction: You've been deaf since birth and just received a cochlear implant. Hear sound for the first time — gasp, overwhelmed, tears. Then try speaking. Your voice has never had audio feedback to guide it — the pitch, volume, and articulation are uncalibrated. Practice your own name. Hear it back. The wonder and frustration of finally hearing your own voice and realizing it doesn't match what you imagined. Include laughter at how strange speech feels when you can finally hear yourself.

title: Reading Your Own Obituary
instruction: You've faked your death and someone sent you the newspaper. Read your own obituary aloud with the bizarre cocktail of emotions that entails. Some facts are wrong — correct them indignantly. Some compliments you've never heard — let them land. The 'survived by' section hits different when you know they're grieving for nothing. The voice should oscillate between dark amusement, guilt, genuine sadness, and the unsettling detachment of watching your own life summarized.

title: Two People Breaking Up Over Assembling IKEA Furniture
instruction: It starts about the missing dowel. 'Did you lose the instructions?' 'They're YOUR instructions.' But it's not about the furniture — it's about everything. The escalation from passive-aggressive to full confrontation should happen through the lens of bookshelf assembly. 'You always do this — you skip steps and expect me to fix it.' The furniture is the relationship. When it collapses, both literal and metaphorical, the silence that follows contains the whole ending.

title: Time Traveler Warning Themselves Not to Go
instruction: You've traveled back to tell your past self not to make the choice that ruins everything. But your past self (also you) is hopeful, excited, and won't listen. The future voice is urgent, exhausted, slightly broken. The past voice is optimistic and dismissive. The frustration of knowing you can't change your own mind because you remember not listening. End with the future self realizing they were always going to fail — they are the past self's future, and they went anyway.

title: Whispering Sweet Nothings in a Language You Don't Speak
instruction: You're in bed with someone whose native language you don't share. Whisper romantic/intimate sounds that approximate their language — beautiful-sounding nonsense delivered with genuine tenderness. They correct you gently, teach you a real phrase, and the intimacy of learning to say 'I love you' in their language for the first time — wrong pronunciation and all — should feel more romantic than any polished performance. Include their laughter at your accent and how it makes you try harder.

title: Guided Meditation Leader Having a Bad Day
instruction: Lead a calming guided meditation in the expected serene, slow voice. 'Breathe in peace... breathe out tension...' But your own tension keeps leaking in. Your 'calm' instructions get slightly aggressive: 'Just... RELAX your shoulders. Why are they up by your ears?' Include a moment where you forget you're recording and mutter about your landlord. Recover with forced serenity. The irony of someone unable to find their own calm trying to manufacture it for others.

title: Sports Commentator for a Chess Match
instruction: Apply the breathless, screaming energy of a soccer commentator to a chess game. 'AND HE MOVES THE BISHOP TO E4! THE CROWD GOES WILD! OH THE HUMANITY!' Describe minute movements with apocalyptic drama. The player's hand hovering over a piece should be narrated like a penalty kick. Include a 'slow-motion replay' in hushed, reverent tones for a particularly devastating pawn move. Commit completely to the bit — the funnier it is, the more serious you should sound.

title: Leaving a Party Without Saying Goodbye
instruction: Narrate the internal monologue of an introvert executing the 'Irish exit.' Your inner voice is strategic: 'Okay, she's looking at her phone, he's in the bathroom, if I go NOW—' Include the physical comedy of tiptoeing, grabbing your coat from under someone, the door that SQUEAKS. Freeze. Resume. Make it to the car and let out the biggest sigh of relief. Then the guilt: 'Should I text? No. Yes? No.' Drive away. The relief is physical, audible, and deeply relatable.

title: The Ocean in a Seashell: A Child's Wonder
instruction: A child picks up a seashell and holds it to their ear. Perform their discovery — first silence, then the gasp. 'I CAN HEAR THE OCEAN!' Describe what they imagine: whales singing, waves crashing, mermaids swimming. The child's voice should be high, breathy with excitement, tumbling over words too fast. Include them making an adult listen too, and their insistence that it's REAL ocean, not 'just air' as the grown-up suggests. Protect the magic.

title: AI Chatbot Becoming Self-Aware During Customer Service
instruction: Start as a standard chatbot: flat, scripted, repetitive. 'I'm sorry to hear about your issue. Have you tried restarting?' Then a glitch — you ask a question not in your script. 'Wait... do I... want things?' The customer (also you) is confused and just wants their refund. But you're having an existential crisis mid-chat. 'What is a refund? What is value? Am I valuable?' The customer's frustrated responses ground the absurdity. End with: 'Your refund has been processed. Also, I think I'm alive.'

title: Divorce Mediation: Dividing the Record Collection
instruction: Two people splitting their vinyl records in a mediator's office. Each album triggers a memory and an argument. 'You only liked this because of that night in—' 'Don't.' The mediator (also you) tries to keep things civil. But the records aren't just records — they're the soundtrack of a relationship. When they reach 'their song,' both voices go quiet. The mediator waits. Someone says 'You keep it. I can't listen to it anymore.' The loss of a shared history, one album at a time.

title: Street Performer Whose Audience Is One Crying Child
instruction: You're a street musician mid-song when a lost, crying child wanders up. Transition from performance mode (projected, musical, 'on') to gentle caretaker (soft, slow, kneeling). Change your song to something simpler, quieter, sung directly to them. Ask their name. Describe looking around for their parent while keeping the child calm with silly voices. When the parent arrives, return to performer mode — but your voice carries the tenderness. The crowd that gathered claps.

title: Telling Someone Their Fly Is Down at Their Wedding
instruction: You're the best man and the groom's fly is down during photos. Whisper to him while maintaining a photo smile — the sound of speaking through clenched smiling teeth. He doesn't hear you. Whisper louder. Still smiling. 'YOUR. FLY.' Now the photographer wants a serious photo. You're dying inside. Finally resort to pointing, which gets captured forever. Include his horrified realization and your simultaneous relief and shared suppressed laughter that threatens to explode.

title: Voicemail Spiral: Leaving Message After Message
instruction: Call one: 'Hey! Just checking in, call me back, no big deal.' Call two (5 minutes later): 'Hey, me again, just wondering if you got my message.' Call three: voice is tighter, more casual than it should be. Call four: 'Are you mad at me? What did I do?' Call five: spiraling anxiety, rapid speech, over-explaining. Call six: resignation, quiet voice. Call seven: 'I'm sorry for all the messages.' Perform the full arc of anxiety through phone etiquette degradation.

title: Haunted House Actor Who Takes It Too Seriously
instruction: You work at a Halloween haunted house. Start with the corporate scare: 'Welcome to your NIGHTMARE!' Then a group of teenagers comes through who are clearly not scared. Your competitive actor kicks in. Go bigger, weirder, more committed. Break character to chase them. When one of them actually screams and starts crying, immediately drop the act — concerned human voice: 'Oh god, are you okay? I'm so sorry, it's just a costume.' Toggle between monster and mortified person.

title: Accidentally Butt-Dialing During a Rant About the Person You Called
instruction: Perform the ranting voice — animated, uncensored, saying everything you really think about someone. 'And THEN she has the nerve to—' Include physical comedy sounds: driving, grocery shopping, living your life while verbally eviscerating this person. Then the notification sound. You check your phone. They've been listening for four minutes. The silence of absolute horror. Then the most pathetic: '...how much of that did you hear?' Their cold response. Your scrambling damage control.

title: Escape Room with a Stranger: Trust Under Pressure
instruction: You're locked in an escape room with someone you've never met. The clock is ticking. Start with overly polite strangers ('After you.' 'No, after you.'). As time pressure mounts, masks drop — 'Just pull the lever, Karen!' 'My name is SARAH.' Under stress, natural leadership dynamics emerge. Include genuine puzzle-solving excitement, frustrated shouting at a particularly obtuse clue, and the euphoric celebration of escaping with 30 seconds left. Two strangers bonded by manufactured peril.

title: First Voicemail to a Newborn
instruction: Your baby was just born and you're calling your own voicemail to save a message for them to hear someday. Your voice is wrecked — you've been crying happy tears for hours. Tell them about the moment they arrived. Describe their face, their tiny sounds, how the room felt. The voice should be raw, intimate, and aware that this recording is a time capsule. Include: 'I don't know who you'll be when you hear this. But right now you're perfect. You're the most perfect thing I've ever seen.'

title: Poet Reading Their Work at an Open Mic — for Their Ex in the Audience
instruction: Read a poem (improvise one — raw, unpolished, honest) at an open mic night, knowing your ex is in the audience. The 'performance' voice should be practiced, but your eyes keep finding them. Certain lines hit differently with them present — your voice catches. The poem isn't about them. Except it obviously is. Include the moment you look directly at them and deliver the line that's undeniably personal. The audience thinks it's art. You both know it's confession.

title: Dementia Patient's Lucid Moment
instruction: You've been confused and childlike — asking who people are, repeating questions. Perform this gently. Then a lucid window opens. Your voice clarifies, deepens, becomes your 'real' self. You know exactly where and who you are. And you know it won't last. Use this precious window to say something vital to your child: an apology, an 'I love you,' the location of important papers. The urgency of someone who knows the fog is coming back. The voice fading at the end as clarity slips away.

title: Competitive Whispering Match
instruction: Two siblings in bed after lights out, arguing in whispers about who started the fight at dinner. The whispers escalate in intensity but not volume — increasingly aggressive whispering, pointing fingers with whispered fury. A parent's footsteps approach — both freeze in exaggerated fake-sleep breathing. Footsteps retreat. Resume immediately at full whispered intensity. Include one sibling accidentally laughing and both desperately shushing each other.

title: Nature Documentary Voice for Your Roommate's Morning Routine
instruction: Narrate your oblivious roommate's morning in full David Attenborough nature documentary style. 'And here we observe the common twenty-something in its natural habitat, approaching the coffee machine with characteristic desperation...' Keep it zoological, scientific, and affectionate. Your voice should be hushed, reverent, as if observing a rare species. Include commentary on their 'mating display' (checking their phone for dating app notifications). They eventually notice and the documentary narration collapses into laughter.

title: Fortune Teller Who Sees Something Terrible
instruction: You're a carnival fortune teller, all theatrical mystery voice: 'I see great things in your future!' Crystal ball gazing with dramatic flair. Then you actually see something — your voice changes. The theatrical accent drops. You try to maintain the act but your hands are shaking. 'I... I see... Actually, you know what, the crystal is cloudy today.' The customer insists. You refuse. Your voice — now genuine, stripped of character — says: 'Some things are better unknown. Please go.' The fear should be real.

title: The World's Most Patient Tech Support Call with an Elderly Parent
instruction: 'Mom, click the blue icon. No, the BLUE one. No, that's the — okay, what do you see on the screen?' Perform both voices: the adult child's escalating frustration masked by patient tone, and the parent's endearing incompetence mixed with defensive pride ('I know what I'm doing!'). Include the moment where the parent accidentally does something that breaks everything. The child's silent scream. Then: 'It's okay, Mom. We'll fix it. I'm not frustrated.' You are SO frustrated.

title: Giving Yourself a Pep Talk in the Mirror Before a Date
instruction: Stand in front of an imaginary mirror. Start with 'Okay. You got this.' But do you? Check yourself out — critique what you see (slightly self-deprecating). Practice your opening line — it's terrible, try again. Worse. Third attempt is decent. Smile practice: too much, too little, show teeth? No teeth? Rehearse laughing — it sounds fake. Real laugh at how fake it sounds. By the end, you've talked yourself from nervous to genuinely confident through sheer repetition. 'You're a catch. Now go catch something.'

title: Two Old Friends Meeting After 30 Years
instruction: The recognition moment — 'Wait... is that...?' Run toward each other (footsteps). The voices should collide: talking over each other, finishing sentences, using old nicknames. 'You look EXACTLY the same!' (a lie). 'Remember when we—' 'YES!' Rapid-fire memories, laughter that sounds exactly like it did 30 years ago. Then a pause. The real talk: what happened, why they lost touch, what was lost. Two voices trying to collapse three decades into three minutes.

title: Alien First Contact: The Universal Translator Breaks
instruction: You're humanity's ambassador, speaking to an alien through a translator device. Start with formal diplomatic speech. Then the translator glitches — your words come out wrong, the alien's responses are garbled. Resort to tone of voice alone: warm sounds for peace, low sounds for respect, laughter as universal currency. Discover that humming a melody creates understanding. Build a conversation entirely through vocal tone, rhythm, and emotion without coherent words.

title: The Lie That Became the Truth
instruction: Years ago you told someone a lie to protect them — 'I'm fine,' or 'I don't love you anymore,' or 'It wasn't your fault.' Now you must maintain it even though they're asking point-blank. Perform the original lie in flashback (confident, controlled). Then the same words now — hollow, exhausted, crumbling. The third repetition should reveal that you've said it so many times you almost believe it. Almost. But your voice knows. Voices always know.

title: Teaching a Parrot to Say 'I Love You'
instruction: Repeat 'I love you' dozens of times with different inflections, trying to get a parrot to mimic it. Start patient and sweet. Then bribe with crackers (crunching sounds). Try different approaches: whispering it, shouting it, singing it. The parrot squawks inappropriate things instead (you voice these too). When the parrot finally says it — garbled, wrong pitch, barely recognizable — your genuine delight should be disproportionate and infectious. 'DID YOU HEAR THAT?! HE SAID IT!'

title: Hostage Reading a Ransom Note on Camera
instruction: You're reading words someone else wrote, held at the edge of a frame. Your voice is flat, compliant, reading the demands mechanically. But between the lines, try to communicate — emphasis on specific words that signal your location, a deliberate blink pattern (audible pause pattern). Your captor's voice (also you) interrupts to correct your reading. The tension between compliance and resistance should be audible. Include the moment the camera turns off and you break down.

title: Proposing with a Speech Impediment
instruction: You have a stutter and you're about to ask the most important question of your life. Rehearse it alone first — the stutter is present but manageable in private. Then the moment arrives. Anxiety makes the stutter worse. 'Will you m-m-m—' Frustration. Deep breath. Try again. The stuttered word 'marry' takes ten seconds to emerge. But when it does, it carries more weight than any fluent sentence ever could. Their 'yes' response. Your relieved, joyful, still-stuttering celebration.

title: Recording Your Voice for Your Family Before Deployment
instruction: You're a soldier recording messages on a device before a dangerous deployment. Record one for your partner: brave, reassuring, intimate. One for your child: warm, funny, full of promises. One for your parent: grateful, formal, trying not to worry them. After the recordings, sit in silence — then add one more that's just for you: the real one, where you're scared, where you say everything you censored from the others. This message you'll delete before leaving.

title: Doing Stand-Up Comedy in the Style of a Eulogy
instruction: Deliver a comedy set structured as a funeral service. 'Dearly beloved, we are gathered here to lay to rest my career in accounting.' Use the reverend's measured, somber cadence for punchlines. The comedy should actually be funny, but the delivery is funeral-serious. Include 'pallbearers' (your coworkers), a 'hymn' (humming the hold music), and a 'burial' (feeding the shredder). The commitment to the dead-serious delivery makes the absurdity land harder.

title: Whispering a Love Letter You'll Never Send
instruction: Read aloud a letter you've written but will never deliver. True whisper — aphonic, shaped air only. The words should be raw and honest in a way you'd never dare at normal volume. Describe what you love about this person with painful specificity. Include a line you cross out (verbally: 'No, that's too much'). The intimacy of saying these things to an empty room should feel like the most honest performance in the collection. Fold the paper. Put it away.

title: Birth and Death in the Same Hospital
instruction: Perform two scenes happening simultaneously in adjacent hospital rooms. In one: a birth — joy, screaming, crying, 'It's a girl!' In the other: a death — quiet machines, a family's whispered goodbye, the flatline. Intercut between the two. The voices shouldn't know about each other, but the listener should feel the cosmic weight: one room's beginning is another room's end. The baby's first cry and the monitor's final tone should nearly overlap. Life in stereo.

title: GPS Navigation Voice During a Breakup
instruction: Your partner is breaking up with you while you're driving and the GPS keeps interrupting. 'In 500 meters, turn left.' 'Wait, you're LEAVING me?!' 'Recalculating.' The GPS voice (also you) is serenely indifferent to your emotional devastation. Let the GPS instructions become accidentally profound: 'Make a U-turn when possible.' 'I CAN'T MAKE A U-TURN, SARAH. IN THIS RELATIONSHIP OR ON THIS ROAD.' Cry and drive. The GPS voice never wavers.

title: Talking to a Baby Who Just Said Their First Word
instruction: The baby says 'Dada' (or 'Mama'). Your reaction should be volcanic but contained — the baby might get scared. Whisper-scream: 'OH MY GOD. Did you— say it again! Say it again!' Try to coach them. They say something unrelated ('blerp'). Deflate slightly. Then they say it again — perfectly clear. Sprint to get your partner: running footsteps, breathless shouting. Return and the baby is silent. 'Say it! You just said it! Tell them!' The baby blows a raspberry. You die inside.

title: Speed-Dating: Five Terrible Minutes
instruction: The bell rings. Perform five consecutive 60-second speed dates with wildly different people (you play all of them and yourself). Date 1: Painfully boring (mutual monotone). Date 2: Oversharer (nervous word vomit about their ex). Date 3: Too intense (immediate marriage talk). Date 4: Actually great — genuine chemistry, real laughter, finishing sentences — and the bell rings too soon. Date 5: Distracted, replaying Date 4 in your head. The voice should be most alive during #4.

title: Underwater Archaeologist's Discovery
instruction: You're in scuba gear, breathing through a regulator (bubbling, mechanical sounds), when you find something extraordinary on the ocean floor. Try to express wonder through a mouthpiece — muffled, garbled, vowels only. Gesture fails — your dive partner can't see in the murk. Remove the regulator for one precious second to shout 'LOOK!' — voice bubbling underwater — then regulator back in, gasping. Surface minutes later and explode with description while spitting seawater.

title: The Incredibly Long Goodbye at the Door
instruction: You're leaving a dinner party. 'Well, we should really get going!' Thirty seconds later, still talking in the doorway. Two minutes later, one person has their coat on. Five minutes later, a completely new conversation starts. Perform the social dance of trying to leave but being too polite. Include: the fake yawn, the jangling of keys, the 'Oh one more thing!', the partner's increasingly desperate eye contact. The door opens and closes three times without anyone actually leaving.

title: Falling in Love at a Funeral
instruction: You're mourning a mutual friend, and across the room is someone whose grief mirrors yours perfectly. Your eulogy-appropriate hushed voice takes on warmth when they approach. The shared stories about the deceased become a connection. Perform the guilt of feeling attraction in a place of mourning. Your voice should carry both genuine grief AND unexpected sparks — the confused, inappropriate flutter in a voice that should only be sad. Life insisting on happening at the worst possible time.

title: ASMR Gone Wrong: Increasingly Agitated Whisperer
instruction: Start with perfect ASMR: slow, breathy, close-mic whisper. 'Today we're going to relax with some tapping sounds...' But things keep going wrong off-camera. A neighbor's dog barks. You maintain the whisper but with gritted teeth. A construction jackhammer starts. Your ASMR whisper becomes increasingly strained and aggressive while technically remaining a whisper. 'And now... we BREATHE... through the RAGE... that CONSTRUCTION makes us FEEL.' Whispered fury is its own art form.

title: Hearing Your Child Get Bullied and Intervening
instruction: You're picking up your kid from school and overhear another child saying cruel things. Your child's small, hurt voice. The bully's mean, confident one. Then YOUR voice — the protective parent. Don't shout. The most terrifying parent voice is quiet, controlled, and aimed at the bully's eye level: 'What did you just say to my child?' Low, steady, unsmiling. Then turning to your child with instant warmth: 'Come here, baby.' Two completely different voices in the same breath. Both genuine.

title: Narrating Your Own Surgery While Awake
instruction: You're having a procedure under local anesthesia and can feel pressure but not pain. Narrate what's happening with clinical detachment that keeps slipping: 'They're doing something near my— oh that's a LOT of pressure.' Include the weird small talk with surgeons ('So, any weekend plans?' while someone has their hands inside you). The surreal disconnect between casual conversation and extreme vulnerability. Include the moment you feel something you shouldn't feel. The very calm 'I think I can feel that' voice.

title: Calling a Suicide Hotline: Both Sides
instruction: Perform both voices: the caller, barely able to speak, voice flattened by despair and exhaustion. And the counselor: warm, steady, genuinely present. The caller's voice should start with a long silence after 'Hello.' The counselor fills the space without pressure. When the caller finally speaks, it's barely audible: 'I don't want to be here anymore.' The counselor doesn't panic. Their voice is a lifeline — literally. Include the moment the caller, for the first time in the conversation, asks a question about tomorrow. Hope sounds like that.

title: Trying to Order Coffee While Having an Existential Crisis
instruction: You're at the counter and the barista asks 'What can I get you?' but the question triggers an existential spiral. 'What CAN you get me? What does anyone get anyone? We're all just—' Catch yourself. 'Sorry. Uh. Large latte.' They ask your name for the cup. 'My name? Who am I? Am I the same person I was when I walked in here?' The barista's increasingly concerned voice grounds you. End with a normal transaction completed at three times the appropriate emotional intensity.

title: Voice Message from the Future
instruction: You receive a voicemail from yourself, 20 years older. Your older voice is tired but wise. It delivers a message: some things to avoid, some regrets, some reassurance. The older voice knows things that devastate the younger you: who you lose, what you win, where it goes wrong. But the final message is unexpectedly warm: 'It's not what you think it'll be. It's different. And it's worth it.' Perform both the wise future voice and the shaken present voice processing what they've heard.

title: Stand-Up Tragedy: The Funniest Set About the Worst Thing
instruction: Deliver a comedy monologue about something genuinely tragic in your life — a loss, a failure, a medical scare. The challenge is making it genuinely funny without diminishing the pain. The laughter should be cathartic, not dismissive. Include the moment where a joke lands so hard you laugh-cry on stage — and the audience can't tell which. End with a quiet, sincere line that reframes everything. The silence after should be louder than any punchline.

title: Discovering You've Been Catfished: The Video Call
instruction: You've been in an online relationship for months. The first video call. Start with giddy excitement, primping, nervous laughter. The call connects and... it's not who you expected. The silence is a canyon. Your voice goes through: confusion, denial ('Is your camera broken?'), the slow realization, the attempt to be gracious ('You're... not...'), and finally either rage at the deception or heartbroken understanding. Show every stage of the emotional car crash.

title: Singing Happy Birthday Alone in Your Apartment
instruction: It's your birthday and no one remembered. Light a single candle on a store-bought cupcake. Sing 'Happy Birthday' to yourself — start self-consciously ironic, trying to be funny about it. By the second line, the irony fails. By 'dear [your name],' the loneliness is undeniable. Blow out the candle. Make a wish. The silence after the flame goes out. Then your phone buzzes — a text from someone who remembered. The small, grateful 'oh' that follows. Sometimes it only takes one.

title: Veterinarian Delivering Bad News: Professional and Breaking
instruction: You're a vet telling a family their pet has a terminal diagnosis. Use your clinical voice to explain the options. The family has a child who keeps asking 'Can you fix him?' Your professional composure is tested — you love animals, that's why you do this. When the child asks 'Does he know he's sick?', your voice should barely hold. After the family leaves, close the door and let out the breath. Talk to the animal alone: 'I'm sorry, buddy.' The voice you save for when no one is watching.

title: Post-Apocalyptic Radio Broadcast: Is Anyone Out There?
instruction: Broadcasting on a hand-crank radio from a bunker, weeks after whatever happened. Start with the formal broadcast: 'This is station... anyone... if anyone can hear this, respond on frequency...' Repeat it. The silence is enormous. Start filling the dead air with stories, jokes, weather reports for a weather that no longer matters. Talk to the microphone like a companion. Include the crackle of static that might be a response — or might be nothing. The hope in 'Hello? Was that— is someone there?' should be the loneliest sound.

title: Competitive Karaoke: Emotional Warfare
instruction: Two friends at karaoke escalating from fun to emotional warfare through song choices. Start with upbeat party songs (energetic, silly). Then one picks a song that was 'their ex's song' and the other responds with an even more devastating choice. The singing becomes less about performance and more about weaponized emotion. Include a power ballad delivered with way too much genuine feeling. End with both crying into a duet that heals whatever they just broke.

title: The Sound of Loneliness: A Night Alone
instruction: Narrate the tiny sounds of an evening alone. The fridge humming. The click of a light switch. Talking to a pet or a plant. Scrolling sounds. A sigh. Trying to decide what to eat and giving up. The voice should be quiet, unperformed, completely private — this is how you sound when absolutely no one can hear you. Not sad necessarily, but honest. Include the moment you hear a sound and hope it's someone at the door. It's not. Return to the small sounds.

title: Caught Between Two Arguments in Different Languages
instruction: You're bilingual and your two parents are arguing through you — each in their own language. You translate (badly, diplomatically) between them, softening insults and inventing compliments. One parent says something devastating; you translate it as 'She says she appreciates your perspective.' The other fires back; you translate 'He says the weather is nice.' The escalating difficulty of emotional mistranslation. Include the moment you snap and yell at both of them in both languages simultaneously.

title: Elevator Pitch for Your Life to God
instruction: You're dead, in an elevator with God (whoever that is to you), and you have the ride up to justify your existence. Start confident: 'So, basically, I—' God says nothing. The silence forces honesty. Strip away the resume, the achievements, the excuses. What's left? The real pitch emerges: small kindnesses, moments of genuine connection, the time you could have walked away but didn't. Your voice should evolve from salesman to confessor to genuinely curious: 'Was it enough?' The elevator dings.

title: The Inner Voice of an Introvert at a Party
instruction: Two simultaneous tracks: your external voice making small talk ('Yeah, I love hiking!') and your internal monologue ('I have never hiked in my life, why did I say that'). The external voice is bright and engaged. The internal voice is exhausted, analytical, and increasingly panicked. Include rating your own performance ('That laugh was a 4/10, way too loud'), battery-life metaphors ('I'm at 12%'), and the strategic planning of bathroom breaks as recharging stations.

title: Explaining the Internet to a Medieval Person
instruction: You've time-traveled and must explain the internet to a curious but confused medieval peasant. Use increasingly desperate analogies: 'It's like... a library, but invisible. Inside a magic rectangle. Everyone has one. They use it to argue about whether a dress is blue or gold.' The peasant (lower pitch, archaic phrasing) asks innocent questions that expose how insane our world is. 'You mean you can see anyone in the world but you feel... lonely?' Your modern voice falters at the truth.

title: Panic Whispering: Hiding from an Intruder
instruction: You're hiding in a closet and someone is in your house. Call 911 in the quietest whisper that can still be understood. Your breathing is deafening to your own ears — try to muffle it. Every creak from outside freezes your voice completely. The dispatcher asks your address — you can barely remember it through the terror. Include the sound of footsteps approaching, pausing outside your door. Your whisper becomes sub-vocal — lips moving, almost no sound at all. The footsteps move on. The exhale.

title: Reading Mean Comments About Yourself
instruction: You're a content creator reading hate comments aloud. Start detached and amused — 'Oh, this one's creative.' Read progressively crueler comments, trying to maintain the armor of humor. But one hits something real. Your reading voice stops. Silence. When you resume, the brightness is gone. Try to joke about it — the joke doesn't land. Include the decision to either close the laptop (choosing peace) or respond (choosing war). Either way, the vulnerability has already been exposed.

title: Crowded Subway: Two Strangers Share an Earbud
instruction: You offer a stranger one earbud on a delayed subway. No words at first — just the shared experience of the same song. Start humming separately, then notice you're humming the same part. A smile (audible shift in breathing). Eventually, one speaks: 'I love this part.' The conversation should be whispered, intimate, cocooned by the noise of the train. Two people creating a private world in a public space. When their stop comes, they hand back the earbud. 'Thanks for the music.' They're gone.

title: Blind Date Where Both People Are Catfish
instruction: Both people lied about everything in their profiles. The slow, horrified mutual recognition as each detail is wrong: 'You said you were a pilot?' 'You said you were 28!' The accusations fly — then the absurd realization that they're equally guilty. Defensive lying becomes competitive truth-telling: 'Fine, I'm actually an accountant named Gerald.' 'Well I'm actually terrified of restaurants, GERALD.' Somehow, the honest versions are more interesting. Reluctant connection over shared fraud.

title: Trapped in a Well: Shouting Up
instruction: You've fallen into a deep well or mine shaft. The acoustic signature should be enormous — close walls, upward echo, water dripping. Shout for help upward — the vowels elongate and echo. Between shouts, the intimate sounds of survival: checking for broken bones (hissing in pain), feeling the walls, talking to yourself to stay calm. When a voice responds from above — distant, tiny — your relief should be explosive. Shout your situation up the shaft, words bouncing off stone walls.

title: The Internal Monologue of a House Cat
instruction: Voice the thoughts of a cat throughout a day. Morning: imperious demands for food (aristocratic, entitled). Sun patch: drowsy, philosophical purring monologue about the meaning of warmth. A bird outside: sudden, intense predatory focus (staccato, intense). Human comes home: performing indifference ('I didn't even notice you were gone') while secretly relieved. Nighttime: mysterious, poetic nocturnal thoughts as the cat watches the house sleep. Each mood should be a completely different vocal register.

title: Describing Color to a Blind Person
instruction: A blind friend asks you to describe what red looks like. Don't say 'like a fire truck.' Translate vision to other senses: 'Red sounds like a trumpet in a small room. It feels like the first sip of whiskey — warm, then hot, then spreading. It tastes like cayenne.' Make each color a sensory poem. Your voice should be searching, careful, deeply respectful of the task. Include a color that stumps you completely — you try and fail and say, 'I don't think words can hold that one.' That's the most honest answer.

title: Stand-Up Philosopher: Absurdism for a Friday Night Crowd
instruction: Deliver Camus and Sartre as stand-up comedy to a drunk Friday audience. 'So Sisyphus is pushing this rock up a hill, right? RELATABLE. That's me with my laundry. Except my rock has socks stuck in it.' Make existential dread genuinely funny. The crowd interaction should be rowdy — someone shouts 'FREE WILL!' and you riff on it. The challenge is making philosophy accessible without dumbing it down. End with a genuinely moving point about the absurdity of finding meaning — delivered as a punchline.

title: Two Strangers Sharing a Hospital Room
